issues.description: Condition is correct but reads backwards; invert to express intent directly.
issues.detail: `!(nodeName === 'layer' && typeof node.nodes === 'undefined')` is a double-negative for 'this is a layer statement (no block)'. Rewrite as `!(nodeName === 'layer' && !node.nodes)` or, better, pull it into a named local: `const isLayerStatement = nodeName === 'layer' && !node.nodes`. Same diff size, reads forward. Good taste is removing the special case from the reader's head.

PostCSS containers either have a `nodes` array or they don't. `typeof === 'undefined'` is the long way around. `!node.nodes` is what the rest of this codebase tends to write. Match the surrounding voice.

issues.description: Test covers `@layer foo {}` but not `@layer {}` or nested layer blocks.
issues.detail: The bug is 'layer with a block'. One fixture covers named-with-block. Add the anonymous-block case `@layer {}` and at minimum a passing case for the statement form `@layer foo, bar;` so the regression net catches the inverse mistake later. One more fixture, two lines each. Cheap.

review.summary: Small, scoped, one-thing patch with a changeset and a regression test. That is what a patch should look like. The fix is correct: a `@layer` statement (no block) is still allowed before `@import` per spec, a `@layer` with a block is not, and the diff distinguishes them by presence of `node.nodes`. My complaints are taste, not correctness: the condition is written as a double-negative with `typeof === 'undefined'` instead of a forward-reading `!node.nodes`, and the test fixture covers only one of the three layer shapes worth pinning. NEEDS-WORK on readability; the logic itself lands.
